stem: The meaning of the word Bantai during the Medieval period was?
expl: In the medieval period, the term Bantai referred to a method of revenue assessment in which the actual produce was divided between the state and the cultivator. Sher Shah Suri adopted three systems for revenue assessment—(1) Nashq or Muqta‘i or Kanqut, (2) Cash assessment or Zabti, and (3) Galla Bakhshi or Batai (Bantai). Bantai was of three types— (1) Khet Batai, (2) Lang Batai, and (3) Ras Batai.

stem: Who introduced ‘Do-aspa and Sih-aspa’ system?
expl: The ‘Do-Aspa and Sih-Aspa’ system was introduced by Jahangir. Under it, mansabdars had to maintain a larger force without any increase in their zat rank. (i) Do-Aspa—In this, mansabdars had to keep horses double the number of their ‘sawar’ rank. (ii) Sih-Aspa—In this, mansabdars had to keep horses three times the number of their sawar rank.

stem: In the Mughal administration ‘Muhtasib’ was –
expl: In administration, the Muhtasib was the officer of the department for inspection of public conduct. His duty was to maintain high moral standards among the people. To keep public conduct pure, Akbar imposed restrictions on the open and uncontrolled trade of liquor and prohibited prostitutes from residing in cities. Prostitutes were expelled from the city and settled at a new place, which was named ‘Shaitanpuri’.

stem: ‘Madad-e-Mash’ indicates in Mughal administration –

options.label: b
options.text: Revenue free land granted to a learned person

expl: In the Mughal administration, the revenue-free grant of land given to scholars and religious persons was called ‘Madad-e-Maash’. It was also known as ‘Suyurghal’. The inspection of all donated lands was done by the Sadr, and it was also the Sadr’s responsibility to ensure that these grants were not misused. This land was non-transferable, and it remained with the grantee on a hereditary basis.

stem: In Mughal administration, the 'Chief Qazi' was -
expl: The ‘Chief Qazi’ (Qazi-ul-Quzat) was the principal Qazi and the head of the judicial department.

stem: In medieval India, why was the mansabdari system introduced?

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: The Mansabdari system was a special administrative system introduced by the Mughal ruler Akbar. A mansab determined three things—(1) the officer’s order of precedence, (2) the pay scale, and (3) military responsibility. Under military responsibility, a mansabdar had to maintain soldiers according to his mansab. Through this system, the state placed the direct responsibility of recruitment and maintenance of soldiers upon the mansabdars, in return for which the mansabdar was granted cash or a jagir.

stem: European paintings were introduced in the court of :

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/ More than one of the above

expl: European painting entered Akbar’s court through the Portuguese, from whom Mughal painters adopted two special features— 1 - Depiction of a particular individual 2 - Making the objects shown in the front of the scene in a smaller size. The development of painting began during Humayun’s reign. In Akbar’s reign, European painting influenced the Mughal painting style. In Akbar’s court, Miskin was a painter of the European style. During Akbar’s time, Daswanth was a leading painter. Jahangir’s reign is called the Golden Age (Golden Period) of Mughal painting.

stem: 'Daswant and Basawan' the famous painters were courtiers of Mughal emperor :

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: “Daswanth and Basawan” were painters of Akbar’s period. Daswanth, who was the son of a kahar, impressed Akbar so much with his work that he helped him become “a leading painter of his time.” Later, however, this great painter became mentally disturbed and committed suicide in 1584 A.D. The names of Akbar’s painters were listed by Abul Fazl in his book Ain-i-Akbari, such as—Daswanth, Basawan, Keshu/Keshav Lal, Mukund, Miskin, Farukh, Kalamak, Madhav, Jagannath, Mahesh, Khemkaran, Tara, Sanwal and Harivansh, etc.

stem: Mughal painting reached its zenith under –

options.label: e
options.text: None of the above/More than one of the above

expl: Mughal painting reached its peak during Jahangir’s reign. Jahangir was a highly skilled connoisseur of painting. In the Mughal style, while painting human figures, it was common that in the same painting different painters painted the face, the body and the legs. Jahangir claimed that he could identify the separate contributions of different painters in any painting. Besides painting hunting, war and royal court scenes, there was special progress during Jahangir’s reign in the art of painting humans and animals. Abul Hasan made a painting of Jahangir’s coronation, which was placed on the main page of Jahangir’s autobiography Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Jahangir’s period is called the Golden Age of Mughal painting.

stem: Who wrote Humayun Nama?
expl: Babur’s daughter Gulbadan Begum composed Humayun-nama, which is in the Persian language. Emperor Akbar ordered that anyone who remembered anything about the reigns of Babur and Humayun should write it down and present it to him, so that material could be collected for the composition of Akbarnama. Therefore, many people began writing history, and Gulbadan’s Humayun-nama was also written according to this order.

expl: Ain-i-Akbari was written by Abul Fazl, one of Akbar’s Navratnas. It is the third part of the three parts of Akbarnama. It contains the official account of the administrative system of Akbar’s reign.

stem: Futuhat-i-Alamgiri was written by
expl: The book Futuhat-i-Alamgiri was written by Ishwardas Nagar, who served as a Mughal officer in the Jodhpur region for a long time. This work includes some important events of Aurangzeb’s reign (up to A.D. 1698). It also throws considerable light on provincial administration in Malwa and Rajputana. It contains deep insights into some of the mysteries surrounding his reign; however, the work has at times been portrayed as biased, orthodox, communal, sectarian, and even anti-people. It is noteworthy that in Futuhat-i-Alamgiri, the emperor is shown neither as a supporter of Islam nor as a persecutor of Hinduism. Moreover, neither the conflict with Shivaji nor the events after the death of Jaswant Singh are presented from a religious perspective.

stem: In which language was Tuzuk-i-Baburi’ written?
expl: Tuzuk-i-Baburi, or Baburnama, was written by Babur in his mother tongue, Chagatai Turkish. Its Persian translation was prepared during Akbar’s reign. Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan translated it into Persian, while the first English translation of Baburnama was done by John Leyden and William Erskine.

D. Itmad-ud-Daulah 4. Babar Mausoleum

expl: The Kabuli Bagh Mosque in Panipat, Haryana, was built by Babur to commemorate his victory over Ibrahim Lodi in the Battle of Panipat (1526 AD). The Adhai Din Ka Jhopra, which served as a mosque, is believed to have been built by Qutb ud-Din Aibak. The Allahabad Fort was built by the Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1583 AD. The Tomb of Itmad-ud-Daulah was built by Jahangir's wife, Nur Jahan, in memory of her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg (who bore the title of Itmad-ud-Daulah).

stem: Which among the following ports was called Bab-ul -Makkah (Gate of Makkah) during the Mughal period?
expl: During the Mughal period, Surat was called Bab-ul-Makkah (Gateway to Makkah) because the pilgrimage to Makkah began from Surat. Surat is a major city of Gujarat. It is known for its textiles and is one of the main centres of diamond cutting and polishing. In world history, during the medieval period, it was an important port. It was known as the Gateway to Makkah because many travellers used to depart from Surat by sea route. It was also known as a gateway to West Asia, because Surat was one of the major centres for goods and textiles traded with other Asian countries through sea routes.
